questions.q: How does a game day differ from a single chaos experiment?
options: A game day never involves real infrastructure, only diagrams
A game day runs a full scenario and deliberately tests the team's human response process alongside the technical system, not just one isolated failure
A game day is simply a chaos experiment with a bigger blast radius and no other differences
A game day is only used for marketing purposes, not real engineering validation
questions.explain: A game day builds on the same safety discipline as a chaos experiment but runs a broader scenario and specifically tests paging, roles, and communication alongside the technical recovery.

questions.q: What is Google's DiRT practice, as referenced in this lesson?
options: A tool for cleaning up stale logs in production
A dashboard that tracks on-call compensation
A code linter used before deployment
A deliberately scheduled exercise (Disaster Recovery Testing) that validates both the technical recovery path and the organizational response against real scenarios
questions.explain: DiRT exercises put real production systems through real scenarios specifically to validate whether both the technical and organizational response actually work.

questions.q: What is a "wheel of misfortune" exercise?
options: A lighter, tabletop version of a game day where the team talks through an incident scenario without touching real infrastructure
A random lottery used to assign who is on call next week
A tool that randomly deletes production data to test backups
The formal name for a company's annual budget review
questions.explain: This tabletop version rehearses the same decision-making and communication patterns as a full game day, without any real systems being touched.

questions.q: Why might a game day reveal that a system "fails over flawlessly" but is still not ready for a real disaster?
options: Because failing over flawlessly always means the system is fully ready with no further gaps possible
Because flawless failover is impossible to achieve, so the finding must be a measurement error
Because the team might have no clear process for who declares an incident, communicates status, or notifies stakeholders — gaps the technical failover alone doesn't test
Because game days only test marketing messaging, not engineering readiness
questions.explain: A technically perfect failover with no clear human process around it can still turn into a confusing, prolonged incident — which is exactly what the human-process half of a game day is designed to catch.

questions.q: Why is the debrief after a game day often described as where the real value of the exercise shows up?
options: Because the debrief is purely ceremonial and has no bearing on future incidents
Because the debrief, run like a blameless postmortem, is where process gaps — paging, missing runbook steps, unclear ownership — actually get documented and acted on
Because the debrief replaces the need to ever run another game day
Because the debrief is only about assigning blame to whoever made a mistake during the exercise
questions.explain: The technical scenario itself is only half the exercise — the blameless debrief is what turns observed gaps in process and communication into documented, actionable findings.
